name: Decline Bench Press 3-Second Pause
alternative_names: Decline Bench Press Pause at Bottom
description: A decline barbell bench press with a deliberate three-second pause at the chest. The pause eliminates the elastic energy stored in the pectoral musculature and connective tissues, requiring a true concentric contraction from a dead stop. This powerlifting-derived technique builds strength off the chest and develops the ability to generate force without momentum, which transfers directly to competition bench press and overall chest strength.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench (15–30 degrees) with feet secured. Grip the barbell at standard bench press width. Unrack and hold above the lower chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Reduce weight by 15–20% from your standard decline press weight. The 3-second pause creates significantly greater demand. Use collars. Spotter required.
steps: Step 1: Unrack and position the bar above the lower chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar to the lower chest with control — do not bounce.
Step 3: At chest contact, hold the bar motionless for a full 3-second count. Maintain tension throughout — bar stays on chest but all muscles remain actively engaged.
Step 4: At the end of the pause, press powerfully to full lockout without bouncing or using momentum.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, hold (Valsalva) through the pause and press, exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest instead of pausing — this defeats the technique entirely
Relaxing completely during the pause — maintain active tension even while stopped
Underestimating the weight reduction needed — the pause adds enormous difficulty
safety_considerations: Always use a spotter for paused pressing — muscular fatigue mid-set is abrupt and unpredictable
Secure feet firmly on the decline bench
Use safety pins if training without a spotter
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from lockout to chest contact. Bar must touch the chest during the pause — no floating.
coaching_cues: Press tight even during the pause — do not go limp at the bottom
The pause should feel uncomfortable — that discomfort is the training stimulus
